notes: Ask everyone for one piece of professional good news. Keep each contribution to 5 to 10 seconds. Model the pace.
At the annual, use professional good news on Day 1 and personal good news on Day 2.
Build positive connection and recognize progress. Explain the purpose before the round.
Ask each person to write an answer on a sticky note and share it. Agree on the answers. Return to these at the close. Allow 10 minutes.
The coach’s own answer is “Strategy mapped out. New 3HAG.” Hold it back until everyone has shared theirs, so it does not lead the room. It shows on the “Did we get what we came for?” slide.

override.support: On the Leadership Time Assessment page of your board, enter today’s split across the four categories. It totals 100%. Compare it with your last entry, if you have one.
notes: The team reviews this every second quarter. Each leader enters today’s split. Record how the time is really spent, not an ideal split.
Compare with the last entry where there is one. The founder also has the baseline from the call before Q1.
With no baseline, today’s numbers are the baseline.
As leaders hand off functions and hire A-Players, the CEO’s time in execution should fall first.
Keep today’s entry. The next review compares against it.
When the leadership team is the whole company, skip this slide and ask the owner privately.
Allow about 10 minutes.

override.title: Who owns each function now?
override.headline: Who owns each function now?
body: Start a fresh Function Chart. Agree on the functions: add, rename or remove.
In private mode, each person writes who owns each function.
Show your answers, then agree on one owner for each. Each owner says yes aloud.
notes: At the annual, build the Function Chart again on a fresh page. A year of growth changes who does what.
Agree on the functions first. Add new or planned functions, rename any that changed and remove any that ended.
One person is accountable for each function. Others may be responsible for part of the work.
Finish when every function has one owner who said yes out loud.

override.support: In Metronome: open KFFM. Put it on the screen.
notes: If the KFFM is not in Metronome yet, show the team’s own KFFM from the board. Agree on a date to enter it.
Each owner colors their own function by where its critical number stands against target. Green is on track, yellow is at risk and red needs attention. Red is a conversation, not a verdict.
body: The 3 to 5 key functions are still the right ones.
Each owner rates their function red, yellow or green, by its critical number.
What will it take to turn it green?

override.title: For each lever: did you push it? What moved?
override.headline: For each lever: did you push it? What moved?
notes: At the annual, the six levers are the check on the KFFM. The KFFM is only right if the team is using it to move more cash faster.

Keep the team’s own KFFM beside this drawing. Go lever by lever. For each one, ask its owner what they did to push it last quarter and what moved. A lever nobody is pushing is a finding. Write it down.
Quantity and conversion: every hand-off has a named widget. Each widget is countable, and it is not revenue or cash. Its owner controls it and counts it every week.
Price: what price did customers pay? What changed when you raised it?
Profit per X: has a good one emerged? Take any open Profit per X question to today’s Hedgehog.
Timing: add the days each function really took last quarter. Where did the work wait? Which function added the most days? Compare with the days the team estimated last time.
Capacity is how many widgets a function can handle in a month. A function can be fast and still too small.
Cost: what each function costs to run.
Each critical number should tell the owner whether the function is working. Keep one critical number for each function. Focus the discussion on at most 4.
override.support: In Metronome: open KFFM. Go lever by lever.

notes: At the annual, the team arrives in one of three places. It has agreed Core Values, a draft from a Mission to Mars session, or neither.
With agreed values, read them from the One Page Plan and go straight to the test.
With a draft, the leadership team reviews it, changes what needs changing and confirms it today.
With neither, say so. Agree on a date for the Mission to Mars session and move on.
The Core Values are what each leader rates their direct reports against on the A-Player grid.

override.title: Test each Core Value.
override.headline: Test each Core Value.
override.support: Is it a value you hire and fire on, or a brand value?
notes: A value that fails the tests is a brand value or a wish, not a Core Value.
Ideally 3, up to 5. Test every value.
Allow about 10 minutes.
body: When did you last let someone go for not living it?
Does someone who keeps breaking it belong here?
Would you build a new company around it, in any industry?
Then ask: is an important value missing?

override.title: Does your BHAG pass?
override.headline: Does your BHAG pass?
override.support: Double-check the BHAG you just validated. Read it aloud. Test it.
notes: The BHAG horizon is 10 to 30 years. The third test uses 25 years as one point inside it.
Test leader enthusiasm separately from the whole company’s.
Do not accept an ambition that only repeats today’s business at a larger scale without meaningful stretch.
At the annual, test the BHAG the team agreed on in the Hedgehog. If a test fails, revise the statement and test it again.
Go back to a circle only when the discussion shows the team disagrees about it.

override.title: Is your Market Map still right?
override.headline: Is your Market Map still right?
notes: Put the team’s own Market Map on the screen. The example here is a reminder of its parts.
Ask what changed in the market this year. Look for a new competitor, a channel that grew or a supplier that gained power.
Update the map now, or put the update on the homework list.
override.support: In Metronome: open War Room. Put your Market Map on the screen. What changed this year?

override.title: Your 3HAG line is how you stop competing head on.
override.headline: Your 3HAG line is how you stop competing head on.
override.support: The white is the space between you and your best competitor. You open it by doing more in some places and less in others.

artwork.alt: A line graph for the example subscription company. Twelve market attributes run along the bottom: speed of setup, ease of use, price predictability, reliability, billing simplicity, support from a person, security, integrations, reporting, feature breadth, customization and partner network. Scores run from 1 to 5. A green 3HAG line and a dashed Best competitor line cross the chart. The space between them is white on a gray ground. On the left the 3HAG line is above the competitor line, at 5 on speed of setup, price predictability and support from a person. That white is marked Do more. On the right the 3HAG line drops below it, to 2 on reporting and 1 on customization. That white is marked Do less. Where the two lines touch, on ease of use and reliability, there is no white. A faint line shows Us today.

notes: At the annual, this is a reminder. Put your own 3HAG line on the screen and read it back. This chart is the example.
Say what the line is for. It gives the company white space, so it does not compete head on. It makes the company unique and valuable.
The dashed line is the best competitor score on each attribute. The white is the gap between it and the 3HAG line.
Point to both sides. On the left the company will do more than anyone. On the right it will do less, and it will not compete there.
Where the two lines touch, the company competes head on.
Competitors can copy what you add. They cannot copy what you drop without breaking their own business.
Then ask: what will make this whole line true? The next slides answer it.
Close Day 1. Read back what the team finished today. Name what is still open and when it comes up tomorrow. Then invite everyone to answer.

override.title: How did the year go?
override.headline: How did the year go?
override.support: In Metronome: open One Page Plans. Review the 1HAG, then the last QHAG.
notes: At the annual, the 1HAG is closing. Review the whole year first, then the last quarter.
Updating status in Metronome was prep for today. Confirm it is current before you read the numbers. Record any gap.
Close each priority on two questions: was it done, and did it succeed?
Ask where the estimates were wrong and what the team learned. Use that evidence to set next year’s numbers.
Allow about 40 minutes.

panels.heading: What does it build or move?
panels.support: A differentiator, or a KFFM lever that brings cash in faster.

panels.heading: How much will it move a critical number?
panels.support: Name the number and the target. If it barely moves, think twice.

panels.heading: How soon will we see it?
panels.support: Name the achieved-by date for the measure of success. If it takes a long time to show, think twice.

panels.heading: Who can own it and succeed?
panels.support: One person, with the capacity and the skills to deliver it.

panels.heading: What will it cost?
panels.support: Money, time and attention. Choose the most impact for the least cost.

notes: Ask these six questions of every candidate. Keep the few that contribute most: ideally 3, up to 5. A routine task list is not a set of company priorities.
Builds: fix the cause, not the symptom. An annual priority builds a differentiator or moves a KFFM lever.

Impact and speed are the two warning signs. If the impact takes a long time to show, or it barely moves a critical number, think twice. There can be good reasons to go ahead anyway, but weigh both every time.

Owner: can one person be accountable? Do they have the time, given what they already carry? Do they have the skills, or the support, to succeed? If no one fits, the priority is not ready, or the first step is to find the owner. If only the CEO can own it, name the leadership gap first.
Risk: ask how badly this could go wrong.

Once chosen, ask an owner to claim each priority aloud. Agree on the done-by date, the measure and the achieved-by date. If two priorities compete for the same people or cash, agree on which one wins. Done and success are different dates. The owner finishes the work by one date. The number reaches its target by its own date, often later.
Hover over “KFFM lever” to show the six levers.
Read the new 1HAG aloud, top to bottom, then run the six checks. Each priority must move its number enough, and soon enough to see.
Look at the priorities beside the first 4 quarters of the swim lanes. Check the lever the team picked on the KFFM.
Check that the approved forecast carries the people and cash the first 4 quarters need.
Fix what you can now. Give each open item an owner and a date on the homework list.
override.support: Read your new 1HAG aloud from the board before you move on.
body: Every number and priority has one owner with capacity.
Each priority builds a differentiator or moves a KFFM lever.
No priority invests in an attribute you chose to let drop.
Each measure has a target and an achieved-by date.
The targets keep you on track for the 3HAG.
The widgets support the revenue, and head count is set.

override.support: Take the first 3 months of your agreed forecast.
body: Gross revenue, margin, ending cash, each widget, Profit per X and head count, month by month.
Name an owner for every number.
If a number differs from the forecast, say why.
Is each target big enough to keep you on track for your 1HAG?
notes: At the annual, the quarter’s numbers start from the first 3 months of the forecast the team agreed on. Confirm them. Do not rebuild them.
Ask questions about the math rather than telling them it is wrong. Ask who owns each number.
Ask who owns each metric. Wait for each owner to claim responsibility aloud. Record the owner beside the target.
Revenue is a period flow. Cash is an ending balance. Do not divide every target by four or add up successive cash balances.
Reconcile with the 1HAG: is each quarter’s target big enough to stay on track for the year? If the later quarters must carry more than their share of the year, ask what makes them steeper.
Profit per subscription ramps through the year: $10 to $15 a month this quarter, $25 a month by December. That is the annualized December rate: $300 a year.
If the team changes a number, say why and keep the approved forecast as the team approved it. The next status review asks where the estimate was wrong.
Every leader independently lists what the company must accomplish this quarter to deliver a 1HAG priority, then shares.
At the annual, start with last quarter’s open priorities and the new 1HAG priorities. Add the lever the team picked and the first quarter of each swim lane.
Done is not the same as success. Each priority has a done-by date for the work and an achieved-by date for the result.
Run the six questions on each candidate. Hover over “six questions” to show them.
The team ranks the survivors together. Pick the #1 priority first. Name one accountable leader. If only the CEO can own it, name the leadership gap first.
override.support: What must you get done now to deliver the 1HAG?
body: List candidates: open priorities, 1HAG priorities, the KFFM lever you picked and Q1 of your swim lanes.
Test each with the six questions, then rank.
Agree on the owner, done-by date, measure of success and achieved-by date.
Connect each to a 1HAG priority. Give each an owner, a done-by date, a measure of success and an achieved-by date.
override.title: What else must you get done this quarter?
override.headline: What else must you get done this quarter?
notes: List last quarter’s open priorities first. They stay on the new QHAG until their number has moved.
Take the next candidates in rank order from the same list.
Discuss disagreement, tradeoffs, dependencies and capacity. Agree on the rank together.
An owner claims the priority aloud. Agree on the done-by date, the measure and the achieved-by date.
The achieved-by date can fall after the quarter ends. The owner finishes the work this quarter. The priority stays open on the next QHAG until the number has moved.
Repeat for priorities 2 to 5 in order. Five is a ceiling. Stop when the list covers the critical work.

override.support: Read your new QHAG aloud from the board before you move on.

notes: Start with the widgets, then take the priorities in rank order. The owner of each lane drafts it and the team questions it.
Building the plan together develops the team as much as the plan.
Allow about 45 minutes.
Widgets: a weekly number shows a miss while there is time to act. Ask each owner: can you reach this week’s number? The weekly numbers you count add up to the quarter’s targets.
Lanes: the team sees each week how the owner will deliver the priority. Lanes belong to company priorities, never to a function. Each lane keeps its priority’s owner.

Steps: a step can be a decision made, a test run, a result verified or a checkpoint. It only has to be real and checkable. A live priority that cannot name its weekly work is too vague, or too small for a lane.
Homework: add each lane’s steps as sub-priorities under its company priority in Metronome.
override.support: Work together on the 13-Week Sprint Lanes page of your board.

notes: If the answer is no, change the plan now. Move a step, change an owner or drop a priority.
Lanes show the work. They are not the measure of success. That stays on the QHAG.
The weekly leadership meeting reviews sprint lane status.

override.headline: How are your meetings going?
override.title: How are your meetings going?
override.support: In Metronome: open Meetings. Rate each against what you expect of it: 0 below, 1 meets, 2 exceeds.

panels.heading: Daily huddle
panels.support: 7 to 10 minutes, every day except the day of the weekly meeting.

panels.heading: Weekly 1:1
panels.support: 15 to 30 minutes. Each leader with each direct report, led by the direct report.

panels.heading: Weekly leadership meeting
panels.support: 60 minutes or less. The CEO owns it.

panels.heading: Monthly Town Hall
panels.support: 30 to 45 minutes. Everyone. The CEO owns it.

notes: Allow about 10 minutes. For each meeting ask: is it running, is it working, and what should change?
Rate each meeting that is running: 0 below, 1 meets, 2 exceeds expectations.
Today is the annual. This check covers the meetings that run between planning sessions.
Daily huddle: good news, then metrics. Metrics are yesterday’s widget actual and today’s forecast. Then the #1 thing to get done today, stucks, and anything that can’t wait.
Weekly 1:1: good news, metrics and the top 3 priorities for the week. Then feedback both ways and the dynamic part.

Weekly leadership meeting: good news, values recognition, the widget scoreboard and the KFFM critical numbers. Then the QHAG: numbers, priorities and sprint lanes. Finish with stucks, asks and offers.

Monthly Town Hall: good news, then values recognition. Then QHAG progress on the #1 priority, and how everyone can help. Then financial transparency: what is working and what is not. Finish with one thing we can do as a company to improve our financial health.
Values recognition: name someone in front of the whole company. Name the value. Name what they did.
This is the only meeting where the whole company hears the same thing at the same time.
Financial transparency builds the financial literacy of the whole company.
Show the Team View at a Town Hall only when it changes.
The daily huddle’s facilitator rotates.
The scoreboard shows last week’s widget forecast, the actual and this week’s forecast.

override.support: Write them together now. Each leader shares them with their team tomorrow.
override.title: What 3 messages will you share with the whole company?
override.headline: What 3 messages will you share with the whole company?
notes: Write the messages together and read them aloud. Keep them specific to the agreed plan. Prepare leaders to deliver a consistent message to the whole company.
Every leader shares the messages with their team the day after.
Close the session. Trace this quarter’s priorities back to the differentiators. Confirm when the next daily huddle is. Then invite everyone to answer.
